To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the LOSS SNe are consistent with the SNe in the literature and with the cosmological constant model, (2) there is no evidence for a local "HST bubble," and (3) there is no significant evidence for host-galaxy or host-nucleus effects on Hubble residuals.
(1) the SALT2 light-curve fitter can accurately measure the light-curve parameters of LOSS SN Ia data and (2) the LOSS SN Ias provide an important anchor point for cosmological analyses.
we find no evidence for a significant correlation between Hubble residuals and host-galaxy morphology or expansion velocity of SiII \lambda 6356.

the analysis of the data of the supernovae of type Ia.
the study of the properties of the dark energy and the nature of its origin.
the study of supernovae, and their use as standardizable candles to measure cosmological parameters.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the SALT2 analysis of LOSS and literature data is consistent with the cosmological constant model and the existence of an accelerating rate of cosmic expansion.
the data are consistent with a flat Universe with a cosmological term.
the data are consistent with a cosmology dominated by dark energy with w=-1.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the SALT2 analysis of LOSS and literature SN Ia light-curve samples provides a strong constraint on the equation of state of dark energy, with a best fit of w=-0.86^+.13_-0.17 (stat) +0.11-0.11 (syst) and that the data are consistent with the cosmological constant model.

our analysis of the LOSS sample is consistent with previous analyses and that the LOSS sample is an important addition to the low-z SN Ia sample, particularly for constraining calibration uncertainties.

The main takeaway from our work is that
a low-redshift SN Ia sample can be a powerful tool for cosmology, but the sample must be well understood and well calibrated.
low-z SNe Ia are a powerful probe of the expansion history of the Universe and will continue to be a valuable tool for cosmology in the coming years.
the LOSS SN I a dataset is a valuable addition to the low-redshift anchor point of cosmological studies.
